newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch groups turns up heat in chocolate debate.
newsitem.headline: Dutch groups turns up heat in chocolate debate.

text.p: Dutch fair trade groups have turned up the heat in the battle over use of non-cocoa fats in chocolate, targeting the government's debate over foreign development aid on Wednesday.
Half-page advertisements have appeared in the Dutch national press this week, addressing members of parliament and saying 60 percent of Netherlanders are against "fake" chocolate.

"We want the Netherlands' position to be that no vegetable fats at all are allowed in chocolate," said Mark in 't Veld, spokesman for the self-styled "Cocoa Committee" pressure group which placed the advertisements.
The committee groups the Fair Trade Organisation, the Max Havelaar Foundation, the Association of World Shops and a Dutch shipping and warehousing association.
The Netherlands is the world's biggest processor of cocoa.
A current EU proposal allows member states the freedom to make chocolate containing up to five percent of non-cocoa vegetable fat.

Opponents say countries which now just use cocoa butter may switch to partly using the cheaper alternative, denting the incomes of cocoa growing developing nations such as the Ivory Coast, Ghana and Cameroon.
"We have heard of a Dutch government fall-back position of harmonisation at five percent use (of vegetable fat) throughout the union. That is completely unacceptable," Veld said.

But a spokesman for the ministry of development and cooperation said the Dutch cabinet had yet to make any decision on the proposal but minister Jan Pronk favoured harmonisation across Europe at zero percent use of vegetable fats.
"The minister feels this is better for farmers in the cocoa growing countries," spokesman Sebastiaan Messerschmidt said.
"They (the cabinet) will be discussing it this afternoon."
Veld said that research had indicated that the full effect on cocoa-growing farmers could total $400 million a year, a figure disputed by Europe's chocolate industry.

Fons Kasbergen, head of the Dutch Chocolate Industry Association, cited research which showed the impact on cocoa growing countries would be much less that some envisage since forecast general consumption growth would compensate for much of the substitution.
He said the chocolate industry also disputed the figures on the public's view of chocolate cited in the Committee's advertisements, based on a study it commissioned from market researcher NIPO.
He said the industry association had decided to hand the report over for further independent analysis.
"We want a level playing field, which means member states across Europe being able to use up to five percent non-cocoa butter," Kasbergen added.

Cocoa producers themselves have pledged stop the directive, saying it breaches the spirit of the International Cocoa Agreement which requires member states to to try to enhance the consumption of cocoa.
